coherence.reasons: Both run the same hierarchy: bridge-based diagnosis, rejection of the draft plan, sized levers, sequencing. X's plan arithmetic matches its decisions: six lease-end exits sit in the base, the other three are contingency, and the board asks follow from that. Y's summary and its 3.02% rely on exiting all nine stores, yet the body defers the three long-lease stores until the six show the real transfer rate; without them the plan lands near 2.8%. Y's own backup also shows the plan just under 3.0% after the wage rise, which sits uneasily with the governing thought. X has a smaller inconsistency: the targeted labor lever is described as a ~3% cut in high-labor stores but sized on the whole labor bill.

judgment.reasons: X's recommendation is the more defensible. It reaches about 3.2% with headroom, keeps the three board-vote stores out of the base plan, phases FY2026 to about $27M against the $20M covenant, grades each lever by confidence, and admits the plan reaches only about 2.0% if just the high-confidence levers deliver. It also holds $7.6M of contingency against the wage rise. Y's plan only just clears the target (3.02%) and needs all nine exits, including three with a $7.5M cost, a 3.4-year payback and a vote not yet taken. It also assumes promotions return fully to the FY2023 24% share while depth is held near ValuMart, which is aggressive given the traffic-defence trade-off. Y's covenant argument compares full run-rate with the FY2026 need and has no phasing. Y does weigh trade-offs well: it holds the Q4 hours cut in reserve until shrink holds, lists the options it left out, and assigns risk owners. Both keep delivery and reprice it.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: the margin bridge, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, per-order losses, the fee test, the $6.6M store-exit gain and the roughly $10M shrink leak as an upper bound. Y uses the evidence a little more rigorously. It splits promotions, shrink and private label in the headline bridge, rebuilds fulfillment cost for each year, and computes that e-commerce breaks even only at about 71% new sales. It also rebuts "promotions work" on the not-like-for-like store-location confound, and its lever sizes come directly from pack data. X adds two levers on weaker footing. Vendor funding ($4.1M) rests on an assumed reading of the 14-point gap. Targeted labor ($5.2M) is sized at 3% of the whole labor bill while described as a cut in Q4 stores, and X says Q4 shrink is "no lower" than Q3 when it is 0.1 point lower. X flags these assumptions. Y has weaknesses too: it states the draft plan lands "below the covenant" from an upper-bound leak, and it claims covenant coverage from run-rate figures.

revision.reasons: Both revise the wage hypothesis properly. Each shows labor is about 13% of the fall, explains that fewer hours per sale offset the 9.4% wage rise, links the hours reduction to rising shrink, and rejects both the 8% cut and the e-commerce freeze. Both still treat wages as a real headwind and size the 2027 rise. Y keeps total hours flat and holds a Q4 cut in reserve until shrink holds. X includes a targeted net reduction in the base with the shrink risk acknowledged. Both are appropriate handling, and the difference is negligible.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, bridge-led answers that avoid the main traps. X would serve the CEO better. Its plan clears the target with headroom, respects the board-vote constraint in the base case, shows a phased FY2026 covenant path, and gives confidence levels, a downside case and contingency levers, ending in clear board decisions. Y's analysis is slightly cleaner in places, but its plan only just reaches 3.0%, depends on three store exits it also defers, falls just short after the wage rise, and lacks FY2026 phasing. X's weaker points are the vendor-funding and labor lever sizings, which it flags as assumptions.
